Lamborghini Gallardo With Y-Shaped DRLs, Other Mods, Wants To Pass As a New Supercar - Rendering
11 photos
Photo: Instagram | a.c.g_design
We wanted to say that it’s been a while since the Lamborghini Gallardo ended up in our news feed, but it hasn’t, because we keep dedicating stories to this model quite constantly, and you can understand why, can’t you?
If you said no, you may want to throw away that petrolhead license, because you clearly do not need it. After all, we are talking about an exciting machine that was available with a stick shift, and had a screaming V10 behind the passenger compartment. The natural aspirated engine had a 5.0-liter displacement in pre-facelifted configuration, and was replaced with a 5.2-liter one for the mid-cycle refresh. Besides the six-speed manual transmission, it was also offered with a six-speed automated manual unit.
The Lamborghini Gallardo may be quite old, as production spanned between 2003 and 2013, with over 14,000 units estimated to have seen the light of day in total, but it remains a great driver’s car, not to mention that it still turns heads wherever it goes. Buying one of these means spending from just under $100K to almost $200K for the basic models, with manual ones commanding over $200K easily and sometimes close to $500K if we are talking about certain limited editions with only a few miles under their belts.
Needless to say that the Lamborghini Gallardo needs no aftermarket makeover in order to become more appealing. However, certain gearheads would agree to disagree, and we can understand why, because if everyone wanted their Gallardo stock, then certain tuners would find themselves struggling financially. This story is not about the tuning world, but the rendering one, because the supercar you see in the gallery is not real. It is a permanent resident of Fantasy Land, and has @a.c.g_design on Instagram behind it.
Photo: Instagram | a.c.g_design This machine definitely stands out, and has the ability to confuse people. That’s because while it retains its original design, it has been slightly modernized. For instance, those Y-spoke daytime running lights were inspired by the Revuelto, which is Lamborghini’s modern-day flagship supercar. It replaced the Aventador in the Raging Bull’s portfolio, and is more than three years old. The Revuelto has been joined by the Revuelto SV recently, and this is a rarer model with more advanced features, and extra oomph.
We can also see that the headlights are new, and they have gone down the LED route. The front hood is also new, and so are the front bumper, splitter, and other elements. The side skirts are sharper than the OEM ones, the rear wing is bigger, and the diffuser a lot larger. The taillights seem to have been inspired by those of the Temerario, aka Lambo’s new “baby” supercar, and there are extra brake lights on deck, too, as well as three exhaust tips.
The supercar in question features a dark blue paint finish on the outside, some black elements here and there, and a set of aftermarket wheels. The concave alloys have a Y-spoke pattern, and we can see the yellow brake lights behind them. The Italian flag decorates certain parts of the rendered machine, and the Superleggera name on the lower parts of the doors reveals the initial configuration of this ride.
Photo: Instagram | a.c.g_design This model had 523 horsepower (530 ps/390 kW) to play with when it was new, with the peak output available at a screaming 8,000 rpm. The Superleggera Edizione Tecnica came with 562 hp (570 ps/419 kW) on tap, and required just 3.8 seconds to sprint from 0 to 62 mph (0 to 100 kph). Sure, that may not sound impressive by today’s standards, but between us, it is more than enough for such a thing. And let’s not forget that the Gallardo was developed in the early 2000s, and hit the assembly line back in 2003.
On top of that, it definitely acts more like a Lambo than its successors, the Huracan and the modern-day Temerario, and those who have had the chance to sit behind the wheel and take it out for a spin know what we are talking about. And in the end, the Gallardo may not be really suitable for daily drives, but it remains a very engaging machine, capable of injecting its occupants with a lot of adrenaline every time the driver abuses the loud pedal. Not to mention that it has aged like fine wine, hasn’t it?
Speaking of the design, I very much like the way the Lamborghini Gallardo looks today, and in my opinion, it is best had bone stock. What I am trying to say is while I can understand why some enthusiasts would like the way this virtually-tuned example looks, it is definitely not my cup of tea. But is it yours? Feel free to speak your mind about it in the comments section below, as it is definitely not something that you come across everyday.
